title: AirAsia Loses Less Money, but Its Recovery Must Wait

paragraphs: AirAsia is a low-cost airline with flights across Asia. This year has been harsh for it. Fuel became much more expensive. On Monday, the AirAsia group reported its results for the third quarter. Its loss was about 43 million dollars. That is about a third of its loss in the second quarter.

How did AirAsia accomplish this? Mostly by charging more. Average ticket prices rose by almost a quarter compared with a year earlier. Nevertheless, the planes stayed nearly as full as before. CEO Bo Lingam said the results suggest that "the worst is behind us."

But AirAsia is now a smaller airline. Revenue fell 11 percent from a year earlier. The third quarter brought the suspension of 76 routes. Most were international flights to India, China and Australia, which use a lot of fuel. The suspension of so many routes has helped its rivals. This month, Malaysia Airlines became the largest airline between Malaysia and India for the first time since 2021. AirAsia's Tony Fernandes dismissed the idea that rivals could also take the lead on flights inside Malaysia.

A smaller airline is also expensive to run. AirAsia cut its spending on staff, airport charges and leases. But its fixed costs are now shared by far fewer seats, so each seat costs more to fly. It still spends more to fly each seat than it earns. Expensive fuel is a barrier to profit for other airlines too.

AirAsia is giving back 25 older, more expensive planes this year. Most of these lease arrangements are ending early, which cuts its bills. At the end of September, about 31 percent of the 234 planes in its main fleet were out of service, mostly for regular maintenance. Experts told Skift about another barrier. New planes of this kind will be hard to get until around 2033, so growing again could be slow.

The most urgent problem is money. At the end of June, AirAsia had far less cash than it had to pay within a year. It is working on a financing arrangement of up to 1 billion dollars in new debt. The airline says its negotiations with the companies it owes money to are going well. Fernandes dismissed reports that the government has a plan ready in case things go wrong.

For now, AirAsia is counting on the busy end of the year. Bookings are in line with last year, and its yield is high. Yield is, roughly, the money an airline earns from each passenger. The company calls 2026 and 2027 a "reset" and 2028 the "rebuild," when new jets that use less fuel begin to arrive. Fernandes warned of "more painful decisions" on costs.

So AirAsia has accomplished one thing: it has shown that it can charge more. But a higher yield is not yet profit. If fuel gets cheaper in 2027, as AirAsia expects, higher prices could finally convert into profit. But first the airline must convert its negotiations into real money, and that is urgent.
